name: Left-Wing Nationalism
summary: Left-wing nationalism holds that national independence and social liberation belong together: a people's freedom from foreign rule is empty unless the economic system that serves the ruling power is also changed, and the working people, not the native capitalists, carry the national cause. It claims no nation's superiority, supports every people's right to its own state, opposes colonial rule, apartheid and debt as foreign domination, and treats armed resistance to conquest as justified. Its strands differ on whether to preserve or dissolve national cultures.
scope: Doctrine on the national question only (identity, independence, secession, colonialism, minorities and the means used), as stated by Connolly's Irish Socialist Republic, the Leninist and Stalinist theory of national self-determination, Cabral's and Sankara's anti-colonial nationalism and Nasser's Philosophy of the Revolution. The wider programme of any party or government that carried it (public ownership, welfare, social policy, foreign policy beyond the national question) is not counted unless these texts state it as part of the national cause. Excludes right-wing, ethnic-supremacist and National Socialist nationalism.

keyFigures.name: James Connolly
keyFigures.role: Irish socialist who argued that independence must bring a Socialist Republic.

keyFigures.name: Amilcar Cabral
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde liberation movement who tied national liberation to culture and to social change.

keyFigures.name: Thomas Sankara
keyFigures.role: Burkinabe revolutionary leader who urged a united African front against debt and neo-colonialism.

sources.title: Nationalism
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Nationalism as an ideology that combines with others (a socialist nationalism); self-determination as a core nationalist belief.

sources.title: Socialism and Nationalism (1897)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: Independence without a socialist republic is empty; national history and language worth saving.

sources.title: Patriotism and Labour (1897)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: True patriotism as the welfare of the whole people; national independence as the groundwork of emancipation.

sources.title: Irish Socialist Republican Party programme (1896)
sources.author: James Connolly, Irish Socialist Republican Party
sources.usedFor: National and economic freedom sought together; common ownership of land and resources by the Irish people.

sources.title: Labour and the Proposed Partition of Ireland (1914)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: Opposition to partition; the nation's unity across the sectarian divide.

sources.title: The Language Movement (1898)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: Support for the Irish language revival and for small nations' languages; rejection of conquest and territorial aggrandisement.

sources.title: Labour in Irish History, Foreword (1910)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: The Irish middle class and old chieftainry have made terms with the established order; the working class carries the national cause.

sources.title: Ireland and the War: the position of the nation (1914)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: Irish Neutrality League campaign against Irish enlistment in Britain's war.

sources.title: The Right of Nations to Self-Determination (1914)
sources.author: V. I. Lenin
sources.usedFor: Self-determination means the right to political separation; no national privileges; conditional support for oppressed nations' movements.

sources.title: Critical Remarks on the National Question (1913)
sources.author: V. I. Lenin
sources.usedFor: Against national privileges of any language; against the 'national culture' slogan and cultural-national autonomy.

sources.title: Marxism and the National Question (1913)
sources.author: J. V. Stalin
sources.usedFor: Definition of the nation (not racial or tribal); right of nations to complete secession; national oppression includes restricting franchise, language and schools.

sources.title: Speech before the UN General Assembly (1984)
sources.author: Thomas Sankara
sources.usedFor: Right of peoples to independence; non-alignment; aid and the old economic order; apartheid and colonialism; strengthening the UN; disarmament.

sources.title: A United Front Against Debt (OAU, 1987)
sources.author: Thomas Sankara
sources.usedFor: Debt as neo-colonialism and 'reconquest of Africa'; united front of the dominated; produce and consume at home; armaments.

sources.title: Political Orientation Speech (1983)
sources.author: Thomas Sankara, National Council of the Revolution
sources.usedFor: Class analysis of the Voltaic bourgeoisie as agents of imperialism; a multi-ethnic nation; independent national economy and control of resources.

sources.title: We Didn't Import Our Revolution (1984)
sources.author: Thomas Sankara
sources.usedFor: The revolution as a home-grown, not exported, process; relations with France.

sources.title: National Liberation and Culture (1970)
sources.author: Amilcar Cabral
sources.usedFor: Culture as resistance to foreign domination; rejection of 'assimilation' and apartheid; liberation as more than political independence.

sources.title: The Weapon of Theory (1966)
sources.author: Amilcar Cabral
sources.usedFor: Armed struggle against imperialism and neo-colonialism; the role of the petty bourgeoisie and working classes in leading national liberation.

sources.title: National liberation and peace, cornerstones of non-alignment (1964 speech)
sources.author: Amilcar Cabral
sources.usedFor: Non-alignment, rejection of foreign bases, disarmament and a stronger UN, in Cabral's address to the non-aligned heads of state.

sources.title: The Philosophy of the Revolution
sources.author: Gamal Abdel Nasser
sources.usedFor: Political and social revolution at once; the unity of national elements; Arab, African and Islamic circles of solidarity.

sources.title: Labour and Ireland (1916)
sources.author: James Connolly
sources.usedFor: The Irish Citizen Army as the armed force of Labour, drilled and presented with its colours in April 1916.

missingStatements.text: The struggle for national liberation should be led by working people and peasants rather than by the native capitalist class.
missingStatements.rationale: Connolly says the Irish middle class has made terms with the established order and the working class carries the national cause; Sankara's programme names the native bourgeoisie as agents of imperialism; Cabral assigns the lead to the working classes and the patriotic petty bourgeoisie.

notes: Scope is the national question only, so most statements (economy, welfare, social policy, much of government) are null: the old audit's answers there came from the programmes of parties and governments that carried the doctrine. Answers rest on at least two of Connolly, Cabral, Sankara, Lenin, Stalin and Nasser, and Lenin and Stalin alone are not taken for the whole family (their language, cultural-autonomy and regional-autonomy positions are null; Lenin rejects the 'national culture' slogan that Connolly and Cabral embrace, hence the split on preserving national culture). Themes searched: self-determination and secession, minorities and language, culture, colonialism and aid, debt, non-alignment, armed struggle, race, class leadership, partition. Nasser's text was used lightly because his programme is a separate ideology (Nasserism).
